questions.question: Ms. Chen's class collected bottles for the school recycling drive on 5 days: 4, 7, 3, 7 and 9 bottles. What is the mean number of bottles collected per day?
questions.explain: Mean is a fair share: add all the values (4+7+3+7+9 = 30), then divide by how many days there are (30 ÷ 5 = 6). Two traps: stopping at the total 30, or dividing by 4 instead of 5 — always count the values, not the gaps between them.

questions.question: The afternoon temperatures in Kamloops for five days were recorded in this order: 15 °C, 11 °C, 19 °C, 12 °C, 17 °C. What is the median temperature?
questions.explain: Order the data first: 11, 12, 15, 17, 19 — the middle value is 15 °C. The most common mistake is grabbing the middle number of the list as it was written (19), which is only the median if the data happens to already be in order.

questions.question: Jayden's goals in his last six soccer games were: 2, 3, 5, 3, 2, 4. What is the mode of this data set?
questions.explain: The mode is the value that appears most often: 2 appears twice and 3 appears twice, so this set has two modes, 2 and 3. Remember a data set can have no mode or more than one mode — and the mode is never simply the largest value (5).

questions.question: Priya spent these amounts on lunch at the food trucks near her school: $6.75, $5.50, $8.25, $6.00 and $7.00. What was her mean daily spending?
questions.explain: Add the amounts with the decimal points lined up ($33.50), then divide by 5 lunches: 33.50 ÷ 5 = $6.70. Careful — $6.75 is the median (the middle amount once ordered), not the mean, and dividing by 4 instead of 5 gives the wrong $8.38.

questions.question: Owen's first four science quiz scores are 82, 76, 90 and 88. He wants his mean score over all five quizzes to be exactly 85. What must he score on the fifth quiz?
questions.explain: Work backwards from the mean: the five quizzes must total 5 × 85 = 425, and the first four already total 336, so he needs 425 − 336 = 89. The usual trap is answering 85 (the target mean itself) or 84 (his current average) instead of finding the missing value.

questions.question: A Grade 8 class surveyed how many pets each student has. The eight answers were recorded in this order: 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 0, 2. Which statement about this survey is correct?
options: The median is 1.5 pets, because the two middle numbers of the list are 2 and 1.
The median is 1 pet and the mean is 1.25 pets, so the mean is higher than the median.
The mean is about 1.7 pets, because the 10 pets are shared among the 6 students who actually own a pet.
The mode is 3 pets, because 3 is the largest number of pets anyone owns.
questions.explain: Order the data (0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3): the two middle values are both 1, so the median is 1, and the mean is 10 ÷ 8 = 1.25. The traps here are averaging the middle two before ordering, and dividing the total by only the pet owners — every surveyed student counts, including the zeros.

questions.question: Six students reported what they earned doing weekend jobs: $8, $10, $12, $14, $16 and $90 (one student babysat for a whole weekend). Which measure best describes a typical weekend's earnings, and why?
options: The mean, $25, because it is the only measure that uses every amount.
The median, $14, because with six amounts you take the fourth one as the middle.
The median, $13, because the single $90 weekend pulls the mean far above what most students earned.
The mean, $25, because $90 is real data, so the typical earnings really are about $25.
questions.explain: The total is $150, so the mean is $25 — yet five of the six students earned $16 or less, because one outlier ($90) drags the mean upward; the median (12 + 14) ÷ 2 = $13 describes the group better. With an even number of values you must average the two middle numbers, not pick just one of them.

questions.question: Amara's mean mark on her first four math tests is 78. There is one test left, and she wants her mean over all five tests to be 80. What does she need on the last test?
questions.explain: Turn each mean back into a total: the four tests total 4 × 78 = 312, and five tests averaging 80 must total 5 × 80 = 400, so she needs 400 − 312 = 88. The common misconception is that raising the mean by 2 only needs a mark 2 above the target (82) — the new score must make up the shortfall on every earlier test.
